question: What is the attention mechanism in transformers?
reference_answer: Attention computes weighted averages of value vectors, where weights come from dot-product similarities between query and key vectors: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k))V. The scaled dot-product uses 1/sqrt(d_k) to prevent softmax saturation for large dimensions. Multi-head attention runs this in parallel across multiple subspaces, letting the model attend to different representation positions simultaneously.

question: What is tokenization and what are common approaches?
reference_answer: Tokenization converts raw text into integer IDs the model processes. Approaches: (1) Word-level — splits on whitespace/punctuation; fails on OOV words. (2) Subword methods like BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding), WordPiece, or SentencePiece — learn a fixed vocabulary of common subwords and can handle any input by decomposing unknown words. Modern LLMs use byte-level BPE with vocab sizes of 30K–150K tokens.

question: What is the difference between fine-tuning and prompt engineering?
reference_answer: Fine-tuning updates model weights via additional training on task-specific data, creating a permanently specialized model — effective for consistent behavior patterns and when compute budget justifies the cost. Prompt engineering modifies only the input text (via instructions, examples, or system prompts) without changing weights — cheaper, reversible, but may be inconsistent across inputs or hit context limits. In practice, both are used together; prompt engineering for quick iteration, fine-tuning for stable deployment.

question: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and why is it useful?
reference_answer: RAG retrieves relevant documents from a knowledge base at inference time, then prepends them to the prompt so the LLM generates grounded answers. Benefits: (1) Reduces hallucination by grounding outputs in real data. (2) Keeps models updated without retraining — just update the index. (3) Allows citing sources. Key components: embedding model for retrieval, vector store for indexing/search, and a re-ranking stage to improve retrieval precision.

question: Compare temperature, top-k, and top-p (nucleus) sampling in LLM text generation.
reference_answer: Temperature scales logits before softmax: low temp makes outputs more deterministic, high temp increases randomness. Top-k limits sampling to the k most likely next tokens. Top-p (nucleus) limits sampling to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p — it adapts dynamically to the distribution's shape. In practice, top-p with temperature ~0.7 is a robust default; top-k provides an additional safety bound for extreme tokens.
